A 2018 study led by Sensing Teluguntla and colleagues demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. The study produced high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China, countries that have very different agricultural landscapes.
The importance of cropland maps
Cropland extent maps show which areas of land are used for growing crops.
Many earlier global land cover products used imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution.
Now, with the global availability of Landsat imagery, which revisits each location about every 16 days, it is possible to create fine-scale cropland maps.
A 2018 study led by Sensing Teluguntla and colleagues used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE) to produce high-resolution cropland extent maps for Australia and China.
A problem of scale
Australia and China are very different countries, agriculturally. The former has vast, sparsely populated agricultural regions with large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation that is concentrated in particular basins. The latter feeds a huge population from a comparatively small area of farmland, much of it fragmented and intensively managed.
The Landsat satellite series offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas.
Mapping croplands with Landsat-8
Teluguntla et al. used a random forest classifier to map croplands in Australia and China using Landsat-8 imagery. They also assessed their output against independent reference data.
This included imagery at 30-meter resolution.
The team first mapped cropland extent over the entire country, producing a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else. They then produced separate cropland extent maps for each country and assessed them against independent reference data.
The output of the algorithm is a map showing the extent of cropland cover at 30-meter resolution for each country.
Australia versus China
The cropland maps showed that Australia has vast, sparsely populated agricultural regions, with large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation concentrated in particular basins. In contrast, China has fragmented cropland, much of it intensively managed.
Water allocation is a constant concern in Australia, but in China groundwater depletion is a serious issue in the northern part of the country.
The cropland extent maps derived in this study will help inform governments about changes in land cover. Cropland extent maps produced from 30-meter Landsat imagery have the advantage of better resolution than those made from coarser-resolution data. This will help researchers detect changes in cropland extent that might otherwise go undetected.
Cropland extent maps produced from Landsat imagery at 30-meter resolution will help governments monitor croplands in Australia and China.

This breed’s origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17 th through 19 th centuries, where the local sheepdogs were selectively bred for their ability to herd sheep.
The border collie is active, agile, and intelligent, and loves to have a task to complete. But perhaps most famously, the border collie is known for being an exceptional herding dog.
The border collie is not content to laze away the day by the couch. These dogs need a job to do, and their intelligence and agility make them well-suited for a number of working roles.
Her answers are below.
Why is it important for people to understand the behavior of border collies?
Understanding the behavior of any dog is important, but understanding the behavior of dogs who have been specifically bred for certain traits (as border collies have been for herding) is critical. Border collies, like other herding breeds, have an incredibly strong herding instinct. Their minds are primed to watch animals and steer them in a particular direction, and their bodies are built to run all day long, if necessary. These traits are what has made border collies such good sheepherders over the years. They were bred to be working dogs, and they are likely to go stir crazy if their owners don’t give them enough to do. But, it also means that they can get bored very easily and will work their way into all sorts of trouble if they don’t have enough to do.
Why are border collies so famous for being intelligent?
Do border collies make good pets?
Border collies can make very good pets, but they require a lot of work on the part of their owners. Their intelligence and drive to work make them wonderful pets, but their owners must keep in mind that they are not content to sit around all day. They need mental stimulation, and they need to be kept busy. Border collies also need a fair amount of exercise, and if they don’t get it, their owners may find themselves with an out-of-control dog on their hands.
Are border collies good with children?
It’s also important to remember that border collies love to herd, which means that their herding instinct may come into play if they’re around children, especially if those children are running around and making a lot of noise.
Are border collies good with other pets?
Border collies are predatory, which means that they have a natural inclination to chase other animals. This can be problematic, especially around smaller animals, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that the border collie will chase and kill other animals.
Are border collies difficult to train?
Border collies are highly trainable, and they are particularly adept at learning complex tasks. They want to work, and they want to work hard, and they may get frustrated if their owners don’t give them enough to do.

A framework for our Catholic schools
The Diocese of Richmond Consensus Curriculum is designed to provide a curriculum that is rigorous, coherent, and Catholic. It is a framework by which subjects like science, math, social studies, and art can be taught in a Catholic spirit.
Primary content
The Catholic disciplines provide a lens through which every subject in the Consensus Curriculum is taught. For example, when a student is learning about the natural world, he can learn about God’s glory in the beauty of the natural world. When a student is learning about human persons, she can learn about how we reflect God’s image and how human dignity is an inherent and inalienable quality.
The curriculum will also provide students with avenues to develop a mature Catholic identity, with the ultimate goal of discipleship and holiness.
Catholic disciplines
The following “Catholic disciplines” provide the framework for teaching every subject in the primary grades of Catholic schools:
The Catholic faith
- Faith is the lens through which every subject in the Consensus Curriculum is taught
- The Catholic faith that is lived and taught authentically and with integrity
The Catholic moral tradition
- Students learn that the Church has a role in teaching morality
- Students learn that the moral tradition guides decision-making based on the needs of others, the common good, and the impact of an individual’s actions on the community
The Catholic vision for life and the world
- Students learn about God’s plan for creation and how we are called to recognize it
The Catholic understanding of the natural world
- Students learn that God’s glory can be seen in the natural world and that we are called to recognize it
- Students learn that God’s glory can be seen in the gift of the human body and that we are called to recognize it
- Students learn about God’s order in the natural world and that we are called to recognize it
The Catholic understanding of the human person
- Students learn that human beings are made in God’s image and are therefore called to act like God
- Students learn that human beings possess inherent and inalienable human dignity
- Students learn that human beings are loved by God and are therefore called to love each other
- Students learn that human beings are called to act in a way that respects and honors their dignity
- Students learn that human beings are called to act in a responsible and ethical manner
- Students learn that human beings are called to recognize and respect the dignity in others and to treat them with respect and in solidarity
The Catholic understanding of the world of reason
- Students learn that God calls us to pursue truth and to promote the common good
The Catholic understanding of the world of artistic creation
- Students learn that God gave us a capacity for artistic creativity
- Students learn that God calls us to exercise our artistic gifts
- Students learn that God calls us to appreciate and understand artistic expression
The Catholic understanding of the world of persons
- Students learn that God calls us to treat each other with dignity
- Students learn that God calls us to show love to each other
The Catholic understanding of the world of relationships
- Students learn that God calls us to recognize and respect the dignity in others
- Students learn that God calls us to love and serve others
- Students learn that God calls us to act justly toward others
- Students learn that God calls us to take care of our bodies
The Catholic understanding of the world of faith and worship
- Students learn that God calls us to express our love for him through prayer
- Students learn that God calls us to receive God’s grace through the sacraments
The Catholic understanding of the world of God
- Students learn that God created everything
- Students learn that God wills that we show love to each other
- Students learn that God wills that we take care of our bodies
Students will have the opportunity to examine various moral issues in light of God’s plan for creation, including human dignity, justice, and the common good.
Students will learn from a teacher’s treatment of a struggling classmate, how a teacher handles a conflict, or how a teacher responds to a hard question. Students will learn how a teacher leads the class in prayer and how they respond to difficult situations.
The consistency of the curriculum with Catholic teaching
The curriculum is built upon the foundation of the Catholic faith and will be integrated into every subject area. The curriculum will help students to understand their faith and to incorporate their faith into their everyday lives.
The curriculum will also help students to live out their faith by teaching them how to love God and to love their neighbor.
The curriculum will be taught in a way that is consistent with Catholic teaching and will help students to live out their faith.

Dunkeld is a small Perthshire town, a gem tucked in among the wooded hills on the banks of the River Tay. It was an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland, with Dunkeld cathedral in its present form dating largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. Its attractive centre now has whitewashed cottages with neat gables, a cathedral by the water and a stone fountain in the middle of the square. This fountain dates from 1866 and is the memorial to George Murray, 6 th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864.
It had no piped water. Instead, water had to be drawn from wells, pumps, rivers, and springs.
He had a great interest in trees, however, and all across Atholl his influence can be seen. His great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town.
The 6 th Duke’s great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, as the memorial to the Duke, instead of a statue.
The title Duke of Atholl was created in 1703. Since then, it has been held by the Murray family. The Atholl seat was Blair Castle, to the north of Dunkeld.
The Duke had an enormous amount of power. He was able to influence what was built, what was planted, and how the towns around his estates developed. The 4 th Duke planted vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands. The 6 th Duke brought piped water to Dunkeld, and the town chose a fountain to commemorate him.
The Duke of Atholl had a lot of power.
The Atholl Memorial Fountain is a good place to start a suggested visit. From there, follow the streets down to the cathedral and Telford’s bridge. It takes less than an hour. In 1689, after the Battle of Killiecrankie, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld, and much of the town burned. The cathedral choir remained in use as the parish church, while the ruined nave stood beside it.
The Jacobite army attacked Dunkeld in 1689.
Dunkeld is a beautiful place to visit and spend an hour or two, with plenty to see.

A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples.
Suppliers shipped products to the center, the center stored them, and staff picked orders and shipped them to the agencies.
The non-profit ran its own distribution center, to serve the agencies.
The center added a handling step: every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time.
It was also a handling step that the agency staff did not need: the center gave them the same products they could have gotten directly from the supplier.
The center failed storage, because inventory turned over quickly and demand was steady.
There was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage, and the center did not add any value for agencies to buy insurance against that risk.
The center failed consolidation, because combining goods did not give any meaningful freight savings.
The goods didn't need to be put into larger, more efficient shipments. Suppliers already packed them in the quantities the agencies bought, so nothing needed to be broken down into smaller lots.
The center failed break-bulk, because the goods arrived in customer-ready quantities.
No kitting, labeling, or special packaging happened at the center.
The center failed customization, because there was no on-site value-added work.
The products went from the supplier's warehouse to the non-profit's warehouse to the agency, with no real difference between what left the agency and what left the supplier.
The center failed information, because the center did not give the agencies any more information than the supplier had already provided.
The extra handling meant extra labor, extra space, extra inventory on the balance sheet, and extra days in lead time.
The center didn't solve anything for the non-profit, but it did add a lot to the overhead.
The sensible answer for this case was elimination: have suppliers ship directly to the agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery.
The non-profit could then focus on negotiating prices and coordinating service.
The center's handling step didn't add any value, but it came with a cost: the extra handling, the extra labor, the extra space, and the extra days in lead time.
The center failed every one of the five distribution functions.
If you were a consultant in this story, what would you tell your client?
Would you call the center "dumb" distribution?
No, it's not dumb.

New Zealand
In Aotearoa New Zealand, the relationship between Māori and the Crown is framed by Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi). The authors note that inclusion programmes have played an important role in supporting the rights of Māori, and that revitalising te reo Māori through kōhanga reo (language nests) and wider public use is one of the most visible examples of reversing language loss.

In some cases, your provider may request that you measure your blood pressure for a week before a medical appointment or when you change medications.
Depending on your age and other risk factors, occasional home measurements may also be beneficial if you don't have a diagnosis. That's especially true if you're over 40 or have risk factors such as family history, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease.
What is hypertension and how high is too high?
Normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg (read blood pressure as 120 over 80). A level of 130/80 or higher is considered elevated enough to discuss with your doctor. That's a big difference! A single measurement can vary by 10 points or more, depending on whether you feel stressed, had caffeine, exercised, or took your medicine.
If you have a diagnosis, check your blood pressure twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. For proactive adults without a diagnosis, check your blood pressure occasionally. You can do it every few months or whenever you have a high clinic reading.
When to get immediate medical attention
Seek urgent medical attention for a reading of 180/120 or higher, especially if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or difficulty speaking.
How to use a home blood pressure monitor
These devices use an inflatable cuff to measure the pressure in your arteries. Make sure the cuff is not too tight or loose, and that it is an appropriate size for your arm. The bottom edge of the cuff should be about an inch above the bend of your elbow, with the tubing running along the inside of your arm. Some cuffs fit around the wrist, but these are less accurate.
Hold the cuff at about the level of your heart and sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring. Don't talk or scroll a phone, and don't watch something stressful. Take two readings one minute apart and record both with date and time. Many guidelines suggest discarding the first day's results and averaging the rest.
When to seek immediate medical attention
Do your readings average over 130/80 or higher? Call your doctor and ask if you need an appointment. But these readings can also signal a medical problem that requires attention. A very high reading without symptoms means you should rest five minutes and measure again; if still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
How to interpret home blood pressure readings
A blood pressure below 120/80 is normal in most adults. But many people with normal blood pressure have levels that fluctuate throughout the day and night. If your readings average 130/80 or higher, that's generally considered elevated enough to discuss with a doctor.
If you have a diagnosis of hypertension, your provider will have a goal in mind for your blood pressure. If your readings average higher than your goal, bring them up with your doctor and ask what to do. When your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly.
If your readings are below your goal, that's great!

Agriculture is the largest consumer of freshwater on a global basis, so knowing where crops are grown helps to estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management. As a result, mapping cropland accurately has been a major objective of land cover scientists.
Until recently, however, one of the biggest challenges to making continent-scale maps of cropland has been the tremendous volume of Landsat observations needed. That barrier kept many teams from attempting such work.
The enormous amount of computation involved in assembling a single map from Landsat imagery was a showstopper for many potential users. Scientists and analysts usually were not willing to invest the time and effort needed to develop a cloud-based infrastructure that could accommodate all the scene-by-scene processing and compositing, and they certainly did not want to move all that data from Landsat’s distributed archive to their own computing systems.
Earth Engine hosts the entire Landsat archive alongside other datasets and executes your analysis on Google’s cloud infrastructure. This capability made it possible for researchers to write an analysis once and execute it across enormous areas without having to move the data. The barrier to continent-scale mapping of cropland was lifted.
Using the same methods and models, the latest effort focused on Australia and China, two countries that differ sharply in their cropping systems, climates, and landscapes. Though many global land cover products use imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution, Landsat offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas.
In each case, the cropland map was generated using a random forest algorithm, which is adept at handling many input variables, tolerates noisy data, and is relatively resistant to overfitting. The cropland map has been validated using various sampling techniques and shows good agreement with field data.
The maps indicate where crops are grown; they do not specify which crops are grown, whether land is irrigated, or how intensively it is farmed.
The amount of cropland in Australia and China compared to their respective sizes.
The maps reveal some key differences between the two countries.
This agricultural heartland is a relatively small area that feeds a huge population. Much of the cropland is in fragmented, intensively managed plots.
Despite the differences between these regions, accurate, consistent mapping across them allows for comparisons that national datasets with differing definitions and standards often cannot support.
Knowing the footprint of cropland also helps analysts to estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management.
Cropland change also affects long-term resource planning.
The cropland maps for Australia and China show that continent-scale mapping of cropland at field-level detail is now practical, repeatable, and affordable. This work lays the groundwork for other studies that build on these observations, giving scientists and analysts the ability to refresh their analysis as new imagery arrives and deepen their understanding of how these regions are changing.

The Facts
- Uganda has one of the youngest populations in the world
- Much urban growth happens in peri-urban slums
- Small children are left in the care of slightly older siblings while parents and guardians search for daily work
The Problem
Slum children in peri-urban Kampala face a daily gauntlet of malnutrition, sickness, injury, and exploitation, and a consequent cycle of poverty that is extremely hard to break. In the overcrowded, under-served neighborhoods where they live, cramped and unsanitary housing, poor sanitation, and stretched or absent public services leave them vulnerable to malnutrition and preventable illness.
Our proposal
We aim to break the cycle at several points at once. By establishing community centers in peri-urban slums, we will offer safe, supervised play spaces away from street dangers, information on safe motherhood practices, and age-appropriate early learning activities that build literacy, numeracy, and social skills. Where possible, the centers will be staffed by caregivers and volunteers from the surrounding area, creating jobs, building trust, and reinforcing the sense that the center is their center. Centers will also provide secure, supervised play spaces away from street dangers, and safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers. As families take part in keeping the center running, a sense of ownership will reinforce the idea that it is their center.
A mother who is better informed and has greater earning ability can make choices that strengthen her whole household, while a teenage girl who sees a real alternative to early motherhood can help change the cycle. Informed and economically empowered mothers can help their children learn and grow to be productive adults, and a child who is safe, well fed, healthy, and stimulated in the early years is better able to learn, stay in school, and grow into a productive adult.
Our goals
- Topic support structures that help to keep children safe, fed, and healthy
- Topic support structures that help parents, guardians, local leaders, and youth to make lasting changes
- Topic youth and young mothers to invest in their futures
- Topic the whole community to develop and exercise the skills needed to keep the center going
- Topic the community to stay connected to the center

The traits that make the border collie brilliant in a pasture, though, can make them difficult in a typical home.
A border collie does exactly what it says on the tin: it belongs to the borderlands that lie between England and Scotland. The borderlands were rough, hilly terrain where sheep were a livelihood. Sheep were tended by shepherds who, in turn, were tended by dogs. The shepherd was the breadwinner and the dog was the partner. It made sense to rely on a partner that could do things a shepherd couldn’t.
Although herding behaviors are modified pieces of the predatory sequence found in wolves and other canids — orient, eye, stalk, chase — the grab-and-kill end of the sequence had to be largely bred out. The predator would remain, though, and the sheepdog’s eye would remain an intense, fixed stare that exerted pressure on livestock without physical contact.
The best sheepdogs are willing to take direction from a handler, even at a distance, and border collies are in that best category.
The border collie comes in a wide range of coat types, colors, ear carriages, and sizes. The classic border collie color is black and white, but merles, reds, tricolors, and others also occur.
Adam Telfer was a Northumberland shepherd working in the 19 century. Telfer is often credited with helping to consolidate the border collie type through deliberate crossbreeding. Whether this is true or not, the breed’s origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17 through 19 centuries. The term “sheep dog trials” was coined in 19 century and remain popular today. They allow shepherds to compare their dogs side by side and reward dogs that move stock calmly and efficiently under pressure.
Like any dog, a border collie needs enough exercise to remain healthy, both physically and mentally. This is especially true for border collies. Under-stimulated border collies may show anxiety, destructiveness, or restlessness. Stimulating a border collie mentally can be a challenge.
While border collies in homes may nip at heels or herd family members, especially kids, their herding instinct can serve as a great outlet. They’re brilliant athletes and brilliant herders — brilliant dogs, all in all.

Dunkeld is a small Perthshire town, in its centre, whitewashed cottages with neat gables and a cathedral by the water. The water running to the homes around it was a gift from the Atholl estate, which played a leading part in the rebuilding and later improvements. A ducal family's decisions could affect housing and the village school. In the early nineteenth century the town was improved by the 4 th Duke of Atholl, a powerful presence in the area when Telford's bridge was built. Dunkeld's cathedral in its present form dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. The estate's stewardship of the cathedral grounds helped preserve the site. The water running to Dunkeld's homes was a gift of the Atholl estate. A reliable piped water supply was one of the most significant improvements a Victorian community could receive, reducing drudgery and risk of disease. The woodlands around Dunkeld still bear the mark of these plantings. They transformed the look of the hills, becoming part of the area's identity - and still draw walkers and visitors. The water flowing from the Atholl Memorial Fountain is a gift from the estate, to remind us of the Atholl family's support of Dunkeld.

- A warehouse is a tool. It is a place where goods are stored. Warehouses are where goods wait, and waiting costs money. As such, the first question to ask about any warehouse is “do we really need this?” Most supply chains still have warehouses, and the simple act of breaking bulk – receiving bulk shipments and splitting them into smaller orders – is a valuable service. However, the warehouse itself is not valuable unless it saves more in freight, inventory risk, or service than it adds in handling and space.
- Information provision – including accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking – is also valuable, but it is not tied to the warehouse itself.
- What does it take for a warehouse to earn its keep? A distribution center earns its keep when it breaks bulk, smooths timing, consolidates freight, or customizes product in ways that reduce total cost or improve service. Some warehouses label, kit, package, assemble, or configure products to customer needs, often delaying final differentiation until the last responsible moment. Some warehouses also assemble mixed shipments from many distant sources in a way that cuts freight costs. To justify their existence, warehouses must do one or more of these things well enough to offset their cost.
- The “break-bulk” test is a useful way to think through whether a warehouse is needed: does the customer need smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and is it cheaper to move the bulk to one point first? Office supplies are not seasonal, perishable, or speculative, so there was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage. Finally, the organization did not perform any kitting, labeling, or special packaging. As such, the warehouse did not perform a break-bulk function, nor was it needed to smooth timing, consolidate freight, or customize in ways that could not be provided by the supplier.
- What about providing information? As mentioned above, the information is not tied to the warehouse, and there was no reason that the supplier could not have provided the same information from its own facility.
A distribution center that earned its place ten years ago may not do so today. And sometimes product packaging changes, suppliers improve delivery options, and demand patterns shift.
- If the balance shifts against the need for a warehouse, it will likely become obsolete.
It looked important. Was it?
- To answer that question, consider what the distribution center did:
- It did not lower prices.
- It did not lower inventory. Some warehouses hold large amounts of inventory, and some organizations do need this.
- It did not provide better service.
- It did not provide better information. Information provision includes accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking. The information is not tied to the warehouse, and there was no reason that the supplier could not have provided the same information from its own facility.
- It did not perform a break-bulk function.
- It did not consolidate freight.
- It did not smooth timing.
- Most supply chains still have warehouses, and the simple act of breaking bulk – receiving bulk shipments and splitting them into smaller orders – is a valuable service. If it fails the break-bulk test, it may still add value in other ways, but if it does not, it is probably obsolete.

Blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day, so patterns matter more than individual readings. Consistent timing, rest, and correct sitting, right cuff size, and keeping records make a home device a tool for protecting your heart, brain, and kidneys.
Take-home reading often tells more about your individual situation, but it takes only a few minutes to reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm.
What’s normal?
Normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg.
Getting started
The device you choose should be reliable. The best types are those with an arm cuff (a watch or wrist monitor won’t do). Upper-arm automatic monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices.
Most devices come with a standard cuff, but larger or smaller sizes are sold separately. A cuff that’s too large can read low, while one that’s too small can read high.
Measurements are only as good as the technique. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful. Rest your arm on a table or desk with the middle of the cuff at heart level. Stay still and quiet while the device inflates. A rolled-up sleeve should not act as a tourniquet.
Unless your doctor advises otherwise, take measurements first thing in the morning, about an hour after getting up, after using the bathroom, but before eating, drinking coffee, exercising, or taking blood pressure medication.
When to measure
If your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly. Measuring once a day or a few times a day can put unnecessary stress on you and is usually unnecessary unless you have been advised to do so by your doctor or you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure.
When is it high?
Home readings averaging 130/80 or higher are generally considered elevated enough to discuss with a doctor. A single doctor’s office reading is only a snapshot, but a week of readings gives a reliable baseline more informative than any single number.
When to discuss with your doctor
For a very high reading without symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again; if it’s still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
If you’ve been diagnosed with high blood pressure or your doctor has requested monitoring, take readings for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change.

In Years 7-8 the focus of the Te Reo Māori curriculum is on everyday language and tikanga (customs). Students will learn simple greetings, introductions and conversational phrases. They will also learn waiata (songs) and karakia (prayers or blessings) used in school and community settings.
They will learn the Kāi Tahu dialect spoken in Te Waipounamu (the South Island) where “k” is often used instead of “ng”. Students will therefore learn to say Kāi Tahu instead of Ngāi Tahu.
Students learn how to introduce themselves and their families, talk about food, festivals and everyday situations. They are also taught how to tell the time and make arrangements. In Year 10 the aim is to prepare students for NCEA Level 1 and to build practical skills for use in the community. Topics covered include formal language for speeches and ceremonies, the tikanga (customs) of the marae, including pōwhiri (welcome ceremonies), the roles on the marae and appropriate behaviour.
The junior classes use the [textbook/resource title for Te Reo Māori] and [textbook/resource title for German] textbooks as well as teacher-made materials, digital tools and audio resources.
